nodes.label: Why is counterfactual reasoning important to world models?
nodes.summary: It allows the model to simulate possible consequences before acting.

nodes.label: What data do world models learn from?
nodes.summary: Perceptual data plus action-labelled records of what happened after an action.

nodes.label: What are the three functional categories of world models?
nodes.summary: Renderers help systems see, simulators help them understand dynamics and planners help them act.

nodes.label: What does a renderer do in a world-model stack?
nodes.summary: It generates what a world looks like, but appearance is not proof of physical validity.

nodes.label: What does a simulator do in a world-model stack?
nodes.summary: It models how a world behaves and how changes affect it.

nodes.label: What does a planner do in a world-model stack?
nodes.summary: It chooses actions or trajectories based on state, goals and expected effects.

nodes.label: When does a world model become interactive?
nodes.summary: When perception, simulation and planning form a real-time action-feedback loop.

nodes.label: Are general-purpose world models solved?
nodes.summary: No; generalisation and reliable physical prediction remain open research problems.

nodes.label: What does coherence mean in a world model?
nodes.summary: The model preserves consistent state, identity and relationships over time and action.

nodes.label: What is the visual plausibility trap?
nodes.summary: A world can look real while behaving incorrectly.

nodes.label: What is the simulation-to-reality gap?
nodes.summary: Success in simulation may not transfer to the real environment.

nodes.label: How should a world model be evaluated?
nodes.summary: Evaluate the model according to its function and the consequences of deployment.

nodes.label: Which benchmarks does the paper mention for world models?
nodes.summary: The field has several partial benchmarks but no settled safety-critical standard.

nodes.label: How does world-model governance differ from LLM and agent governance?
nodes.summary: World-model governance must validate the modelled environment, not only content and action permissions.

nodes.label: What is spatial privacy?
nodes.summary: Protecting sensor data and inferred profiles about people, places and behaviour over time.

nodes.label: How should data minimisation apply to world models?
nodes.summary: Collect cautiously during development, then retain only what is demonstrably necessary.

nodes.label: What should world-model systems log?
nodes.summary: Log perception, inferred state and action with timestamps.

nodes.label: What is the central governance principle for world models?
nodes.summary: Govern according to deployment consequences, not merely the model label.

nodes.label: Why does independent evaluation matter for world models?
nodes.summary: The builder's own simulator should not be the only judge of the builder's system.

nodes.label: Why do world models matter?
nodes.summary: They can make simulation, planning, experimentation and embodied-AI training more accessible.

nodes.label: What are the principal risks of world models?
nodes.summary: Invalid simulated worlds can create unsafe action, privacy loss, dependency and cyber-physical risk.

nodes.label: Why might world-model capability become concentrated?
nodes.summary: Compute, simulation infrastructure and scarce action-labelled data favour incumbent operators.

nodes.label: Does a world model remove the need for human oversight?
nodes.summary: No; higher-stakes world-model use requires stronger human oversight.

nodes.label: Appropriate Autonomy
nodes.description: The objective is not maximum automation but the correct balance between agent and human control.

nodes.label: Context Creates Intelligence
nodes.description: Data becomes useful when connected to purpose, history, ownership, confidence, and impact.

nodes.label: Decision Quality
nodes.description: The value of intelligence is measured by the quality and speed of decisions it enables.

nodes.label: Feedback Loops
nodes.description: Systems must learn from outcomes and adjust behavior over time.

nodes.label: Human Accountability
nodes.description: AI can support or execute decisions, but responsibility must remain explicit.

nodes.label: Signal Over Noise
nodes.description: More information is not the goal; the goal is clearer prioritization and action.

nodes.label: Systems Before Features
nodes.description: Understand the workflow, incentives, and decision structure before adding technology.

nodes.label: Trust Before Autonomy
nodes.description: Autonomy should increase only when evidence, observability, and accountability are credible.

nodes.label: AI Adoption Failure
nodes.description: AI capabilities are available but are not trusted, integrated, or used consistently.

nodes.label: Data Silos
nodes.description: Teams work from disconnected systems and inconsistent information.

nodes.label: Governance Gaps
nodes.description: AI systems lack clear controls, accountability, auditability, or human oversight.

nodes.label: Knowledge Fragmentation
nodes.description: Critical knowledge is distributed across systems, teams, documents, and individual experts.

nodes.label: Low Trust
nodes.description: Users cannot confidently verify data, recommendations, or AI-generated outputs.

nodes.label: Manual Knowledge Work
nodes.description: Employees repeatedly research, summarize, reconcile, and recreate information.

nodes.label: Operational Friction
nodes.description: Work is slowed by handoffs, repeated coordination, manual processes, and unclear workflows.

nodes.label: Organizational Complexity
nodes.description: People, processes, incentives, data, and technology are poorly aligned.

nodes.label: Slow Decision-Making
nodes.description: Decisions are delayed by unclear ownership, conflicting evidence, and fragmented information.

nodes.label: Unclear ROI
nodes.description: Technology investment is not connected to a measurable business baseline or outcome.
